title: Computable trees and noncomputable paths

based_on.title: Basic Computability Theory

based_on.title: Computability theory
based_on.pages: Version 2024-02-25; §23.2, Lemmas 23.2–23.3, p.86, and Exercise 23.6, p.87; halting query and unique-path search made explicit

summary: Separate computable finite choices from an infinite path, and determine when halting information or uniqueness lets us compute one.
abstract: Suppose a program can decide which finite lists of zeros and ones are allowed, every prefix of an allowed list is allowed, and allowed lists have arbitrarily large lengths. An infinite sequence with only allowed prefixes must exist, but a program need not be able to produce its bits. Disjoint computably enumerable sets that cannot be computably separated give a concrete tree with no computable path, even though a program can find an allowed list at every length. The halting oracle can still compute a path through any such binary tree: it detects when one proposed next bit leaves no sufficiently long extensions. Uniqueness gives a stronger conclusion. If a computable binary tree has exactly one infinite path, ordinary finite searches eventually eliminate every false candidate for each requested prefix, making that path computable.
